items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    The paper first scrutinizes thoroughly the variety of compositions which lead to the same quantum-mechanical
                    <jats:italic>mixture</jats:italic>
                    (as opposed to
                    <jats:italic>state</jats:italic>
                    or
                    <jats:italic>pure state</jats:italic>
                    ). With respect to a given mixture
                    <jats:italic>every</jats:italic>
                    state has a definite probability (or mixing fraction) between 0 and 1 (including the limits), which is calculated from the mixtures Statistical Operator and the wave function of the state in question.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    A well-known example of mixtures occurs when a system consists of two separated parts. If the wave function of the whole system is known, either part is in the situation of a mixture, which is decomposed into
                    <jats:italic>definite</jats:italic>
                    constituents by a
                    <jats:italic>definite</jats:italic>
                    measuring programme to be carried out on the
                    <jats:italic>other</jats:italic>
                    part. All the conceivable decompositions (into linearly independent constituents) of the first system are just realized by all the possible measuring programmes that can be carried out on the second one.
                    <jats:italic>In general every</jats:italic>
                    state of the first system can be given a finite chance by a suitable choice of the programme.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>It is suggested that these conclusions, unavoidable within the present theory but repugnant to some physicists including the author, are caused by applying non-relativistic quantum mechanics beyond its legitimate range. An alternative possibility is indicated.</jats:p>
title: Probability relations between separated systems

reference.unstructured: Mathematische Grundlagen der Quantenmechanik, Berlin, Springer, 1932

container-title: Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society

items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    The probability relations which can occur between two separated physical systems are discussed, on the assumption that their state is known by a representative in common. The
                    <jats:italic>two families</jats:italic>
                    of observables, relating to the first and to the second system respectively, are linked by at least
                    <jats:italic>one match</jats:italic>
                    between two definite members, one of either family. The word
                    <jats:italic>match</jats:italic>
                    is short for stating that the
                    <jats:italic>values</jats:italic>
                    of the two observables in question determine each other uniquely and therefore (since the actual labelling is irrelevant) can be taken to be
                    <jats:italic>equal.</jats:italic>
                    In general there is but one match, but there can be more. If, in addition to the first match, there is a second one between canonical conjugates of the first mates, then there are infinitely many matches, every function of the first canonical pair matching with the same function of the second canonical pair. Thus there is a complete one-to-one correspondence between
                    <jats:italic>those</jats:italic>
                    two branches (of the two families of observables) which relate to the two degrees of freedom in question. If there
                    <jats:italic>are</jats:italic>
                    no others, the one-to-one correspondence persists as time advances, but the observables of the first system (say) change their mates in the way that the latter, i.e. the observables of the second system, undergo a certain continuous contact-transformation.
                  </jats:p>
title: Discussion of Probability Relations between Separated Systems

reference.unstructured: Courant-Hilbert , Methoden der mathematischen Physik, 2nd edition, p. 134.
